original_question: Is it consistent that p < t (the Minimal Tower Problem)?
target_in_paper: Section 11, "Cardinal characteristics of the continuum," Problem 11.1: "Is it consistent that p < t?" The surrounding sentence identifies this as "the Minimal Tower Problem."
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official formulation essentially verbatim: it asks exactly whether p < t is consistent, and it correctly identifies this as the Minimal Tower Problem.
missing_details: The draft does not say that consistency is meant relative to ZFC (i.e., whether there is a model of ZFC in which the inequality holds).
It does not define p, the pseudo-intersection number: the least cardinality of a centered family F of infinite subsets of ω with no infinite pseudo-intersection.

It does not define t, the tower number: the least cardinality of a tower T of infinite subsets of ω, linearly ordered by ⊆* (equivalently, a ⊇*-decreasing family), with no infinite pseudo-intersection.
It does not define centered: every finite subfamily has infinite intersection.
It does not define pseudo-intersection: an infinite A ⊆ ω such that A ⊆* B for every B in the family.
It does not define the mod-finite relation A ⊆* B, meaning A \ B is finite.
It does not state explicitly that all families live in [ω]^ω, the collection of infinite subsets of the natural numbers.
It does not indicate that the paper treats this narrowly as Problem 11.1, distinct from nearby variants such as p*, od, and p_κ.
refined_question: Is it consistent with ZFC that the pseudo-intersection number p is strictly smaller than the tower number t; that is, that the least cardinality of a centered family F ⊆ [ω]^ω with no infinite pseudo-intersection is smaller than the least cardinality of a tower T ⊆ [ω]^ω (a family linearly ordered by ⊆*, where A ⊆* B means A \ B is finite) with no infinite pseudo-intersection?
justification: The paper states this problem explicitly, in exactly this narrow form, as Problem 11.1 and calls it the Minimal Tower Problem. The immediately following text treats p* , od, and p_κ as separate neighboring variants rather than as reformulations of Problem 11.1, so the faithful refinement is to keep the question exactly about p and t and only unpack the standard set-theoretic notation needed to make it stand-alone.
